source: Aggarwal et al. (2023, EMNLP) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
finding: Sample answers one at a time. After each, compute the chance that the current leader stays the majority if sampling were repeated. Stop when that chance passes a threshold. The cheap Beta form uses only the top two answer counts.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 models (GPT-3.5-Turbo, Vicuna-13B, Code-Davinci-002). Threshold 0.95. Cap 40 samples for reasoning. Budget cut up to 7.9x, average 3.3x on math, with accuracy drop under 0.1 point on average.
quote: reduces sample budget by up to 7.9 times with an average accuracy drop of less than 0.1%
limits: Needs the threshold tuned. Authors say it is expected to fail where Self-Consistency fails. Samples one by one, so the prompt is re-sent each time.
agent_relevance: Direct template for a code-side vote-stopping rule in S3/S7 (G5: code selects). Cheap enough to run on every item.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency, per-category and per-model tables
finding: Savings differ by task type and by model. Math 3.3x, commonsense 2.9x, symbolic 3.8x, code 2.4x. Small cost in accuracy everywhere.
numbers: Samples used (SC 40 vs AC): math 13.8, commonsense 15.8, symbolic 13.1. Accuracy math 73.2 vs 73.1, commonsense 66.0 vs 65.8, symbolic 72.8 vs 72.8, code 35.2 vs 35.6. By model: GPT-3.5-Turbo 40 vs 10.0 samples (76.4 vs 76.2); Vicuna-13B 40 vs 21.7 (54.0 vs 54.1); Code-Davinci 104.1 vs 49.4 (69.7 vs 69.8).
limits: The weakest model (Vicuna-13B) saved least (1.9x). Weak models disagree more, so the rule keeps sampling.
agent_relevance: Expect smaller savings on hard problems and weak models. Budget planning should assume 2x to 4x, not 8x.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency, stopping-function comparison (Section 5.3)
finding: Six stopping rules compared at equal average cost: Random, Majority-above-threshold, Entropy, Beta, Dirichlet, Chinese-restaurant-process. Beta beats Entropy and Majority; Random is worst. Dirichlet and CRP match Beta but are about four orders of magnitude slower.
numbers: At average cost 10 on GSM8K, Adaptive-Consistency was about 3 points above fixed Self-Consistency. SVAMP needed under 5 samples on average; Boolean Expressions saved 7.9x with no loss.
limits: Gains largest when a majority shows early and when the answer space is small.
agent_relevance: Use the simple Beta rule, not an entropy rule. Small answer spaces (yes/no, multiple choice) are the best case for early stop.

source: Li et al. (2024, ICLR) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency for Multi-step Reasoning
finding: Sample in windows. Stop when all answers in a window agree (entropy zero). No tuned threshold. A control scheme picks window size and cap to bound the chance that the stopped vote differs from the full vote.
numbers: Average samples cut: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. Models GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama-2-7b. Accuracy change vs full SC mostly between 0.0 and -1 point (extracted table is garbled, so per-cell values not recorded). Results averaged over 10 runs.
quote: ESC reduces the average number of sampling of chain-of-thought reasoning by a significant margin
limits: Window size 8 for MATH, 5 for others. With a weak model the stop rarely fires on hard sets (MATH on Llama-2-7b saved far less). Table values partly garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Hyperparameter-free alternative to c01. Windows share one prompt, so prompt tokens are paid once per window.

source: Li et al. (2024) ESC, appendix A.2 comparison with Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Step-by-step stopping pays the long few-shot prompt again for every sample. Windowed stopping shares the prompt, so total dollar cost is lower at equal or better accuracy.
numbers: Paper Table 7 gives prompt tokens, completion tokens, dollar cost and accuracy per item for AC and ESC on GSM8K, CSQA and Letter; authors state ESC has higher accuracy at lower cost. Exact cells not recorded here.
limits: Authors' own comparison; AC tuned by them.
agent_relevance: Count prompt tokens in any stopping design. With a long scaffold prompt, batch samples in windows.

source: Wang et al. (2025, ACL) Make Every Penny Count: Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency for Cost-Efficient Reasoning
finding: Use difficulty known before sampling. Rank a batch of questions by difficulty with the model, pre-sample easy ones once, and give hard ones bigger budgets. Also counts input-token cost, which ASC and ESC ignore.
numbers: Six benchmarks, GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4. Cost cut vs SC: GPT-4 -65.29%, GPT-3.5-Turbo -56.04%. Cost cut vs ESC (strongest baseline): GPT-4 -24.81%, GPT-3.5-Turbo -21.86%. Accuracy comparable. On GSM8K only 3.8% of GPT-4 answers differ between CoT and 40-sample SC (15.2% for GPT-3.5).
limits: Needs a batch of questions to rank. Ranking adds its own cost. Only the two OpenAI models, six arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic sets.
agent_relevance: Supports G12 and S0 gate: a one-shot difficulty pass before spending. For a single question, use the first sample as the difficulty probe.

source: Kim et al. (2026, Findings of ACL) Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency (ReASC)
finding: Count-based stopping treats all samples equally. ReASC adds (1) a one-sample stage that accepts when the first answer is confident, and (2) a stage that weighs samples by confidence (bottom-10% group confidence, self-certainty) with a Beta rule.
numbers: 5 models (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-3B/7B, Gemma-3-4B/27B), 4 datasets (GSM8K, MATH500, Omni-Math, GPQA-D). GSM8K cost cut vs SC: Gemma-3-4B -68.6 to -71.1%, Gemma-3-27B -78.8 to -82.4%, Qwen-2.5-7B -70.2 to -74.9%. ASC on Gemma-3-4B: -62.5%; ESC (w=4): -60.4%. GSM8K accuracy 92.04 vs SC unchanged. GPQA gains smaller (-4 to -23% on small models).
limits: Stage 1 acceptance grows with model size (about 28 to 60% on GSM8K) and is low on hard sets (MATH500 acceptance 7.2% for Llama-3.2-3B offline). Needs logprobs and a held-out set (k=128) to set the threshold.
agent_relevance: Most recent stop rule that beats ASC and ESC. Confidence-weighted stop is usable if the API gives token probabilities; else use c01.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Best way to spend test-time compute depends on question difficulty. Easy: sequential revision beats parallel sampling. Hard: parallel search or beam search wins. A per-question allocation policy beats uniform best-of-N.
numbers: MATH, PaLM-2 style models. Compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute for both revisions and search. FLOPs-matched: a smaller model with test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model on easy and medium questions.
quote: improve the efficiency of test-time compute scaling by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline
limits: On the hardest questions test-time compute gave very little; pretraining was better. Difficulty is estimated from verifier scores over base-model samples, which itself costs compute. Beam search degrades on easy questions (levels 1-2).
agent_relevance: Core evidence for G12. Route easy items to short sequential tries, hard items to parallel diversity, and give up on items with no foothold.

source: Snell et al. (2024) difficulty bins and the sequential-versus-parallel ratio
finding: On hard questions there is an ideal ratio of sequential to parallel compute that changes by difficulty bin. Easy questions gain most from purely sequential compute.
numbers: Revision experiments on MATH with fine-tuned revision model, difficulty bins 1 to 5; compute-optimal curve beats best-of-N at 64 samples with about 4x fewer generations.
limits: Needs an oracle or estimated difficulty; paper notes that predicting difficulty cheaply is open.
agent_relevance: Our S3/S5 loop: first revise one chain on easy items; fan out several chains when the first check fails.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (RaM)
finding: Takes Russell and Wefald's value of computation and uses it as a reward: utility is the gain in log-probability of the target answer given the chain of thought, minus a cost proportional to chain length. Trains with expert iteration so the model reasons only when it helps.
numbers: U(z|x,y)=log p(y|z,x)-log p(y|x); cost = gamma times token count. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: RaM 63.5% accuracy with 146.2 output tokens vs STaR 61.9% with 215.1 and CoT few-shot 56.4% with 253.6. Llama-3.2-3B: RaM 50.1% at 170.8 tokens vs STaR 47.4% at 222.7. 23-45% fewer tokens across three models.
quote: 23-45% fewer tokens generated across three models
limits: Needs training (expert iteration) and answers with a checkable target. Tested on science, commonsense, logic and math sets only; authors say agentic and tool-use settings are untested.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal frame for our stop rule: continue only if expected gain in answer probability exceeds token cost. We can approximate it by code without training.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2025) RaM, adaptivity and transfer results
finding: Test whether the model really adapts or just thinks less. Split items by whether direct answering was correct. RaM widens the length gap between hard and easy. Instruction-tuned CoT stays equally long on both. Savings carry over to an out-of-domain set.
numbers: Hard vs easy mean tokens: RaM 145 vs 72 (50.3% length reduction on easy) on Llama-3.2-3B; STaR 195 vs 128 (34.4%); CoT prompting 222 vs 221 (0.5%). MMLU-CF out of domain: 28-36% fewer tokens than STaR; accuracy 29.5 vs 27.0 (3B) but 36.4 vs 40.2 (8B).
limits: On the 8B model out-of-domain accuracy fell 3.8 points. Subjects needing multi-step reasoning (physics, engineering) saved less.
agent_relevance: Instruction-tuned reasoners do not adapt length to difficulty by default. A scaffold must impose the stop; do not assume the model will.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling (budget forcing)
finding: Budget forcing: cut thinking off by forcing the end-of-thinking token, or extend it by suppressing that token and appending 'Wait'. Forced extension lifted accuracy; the 'Wait' string worked best.
numbers: s1-32B trained on 1,000 examples. AIME24 50% to 57% with extension. Extrapolation ablation: 2x 'Wait' AIME 53.3, MATH500 93.0, GPQA 59.6; 2x with no string 50.0 / 90.2 / 55.1. Control: budget forcing 100% with AIME 56.7 at best; token-conditional 40% control; other variants 0-60%. s1 w/o BF 50.0 AIME; 'Wait' 1x 53.3, 2x 53.3 (33.3 on a different row), 4x 56.7 (36.7) for related rows.
limits: Gains flatten after about 2x to 4x Wait on s1 (AIME 33.3 to 36.7 on one table row). Extrapolation capped by context window. Only 30 AIME24 questions, so one question is 3.3 points.
agent_relevance: Shows forced continuation helps only on hard tasks and only with a model trained on long traces. Contradicts nothing in G11 but warns that 'think more' is task-dependent.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1, controllability comparison (Table 3, appendix E)
finding: Telling the model a token budget in the prompt does not work: it cannot count. Telling it steps leads it to write many short steps. Rejection sampling to a length gives inverse scaling because long samples are the ones where the model was wrong.
numbers: Control column in the method table: budget forcing 100%; token-conditional 40%; step-conditional 60% and 0%; class-conditional 50%; rejection sampling shows inverse scaling.
quote: Token-conditional control fails without budget forcing, as our model cannot reliably count tokens
limits: One 32B model, 30 AIME24 questions for the control experiments.
agent_relevance: Budgets must be enforced by code (stop generation, count tokens outside), never by asking the model to obey a length. Matches section 1 of the schema.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025, COLM) L1: Controlling How Long A Reasoning Model Thinks With Reinforcement Learning
finding: RL (LCPO) trains a reasoning model to obey a length target given in the prompt. Length can then be traded smoothly against accuracy. Far better than s1 budget forcing at short budgets.
numbers: 1.5B model from DeepScaleR. Beats s1 by 100-150% relative and 20-25 points absolute at 512 and 1024 tokens. Log-linear scaling slope 0.24 vs 0.37 for s1. Mean length deviation from target 5.6-6.3% in ablation. L1-Exact about 1% below DeepScaleR-4K. Short-trace version beats GPT-4o at equal length (up to 10 points over its own base).
limits: Needs RL training on a 1.5B model; only math plus some transfer to logic and MMLU. s1 comparison is on a different base.
agent_relevance: Shows a trained model can honour a budget when it is set per item. We cannot train; so enforce budget by code and cap by difficulty (c08).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend far too many tokens on easy questions. Most extra solution rounds add nothing. They produce more rounds on easier sets. A self-training fix prunes the redundant rounds.
numbers: For '2 plus 3' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. In over 92% of cases the first solution round was already correct. QwQ-32B-Preview averages 3.5 solutions on easiest set (ASDiv). Token output cut 48.6% on MATH500 with accuracy kept (QwQ-32B-Preview).
quote: consumed 1,953% more tokens than conventional models
limits: Analysis on QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 only; fix needs training. Counts solutions using Llama-3.3-70B as splitter.
agent_relevance: Key support for G11 and the S0 gate: easy items should skip long thinking. Overthinking is worse on easy sets.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free. At reasoning transitions such as 'Wait', stop thinking, ask the model for a trial answer, measure confidence of that answer, and exit if over a threshold (0.95). Otherwise keep thinking.
numbers: About 75% of samples have an early exit that is already correct; 36.7% needed under half their reasoning. Across 10 benchmarks and reasoning models, chain length cut 19.1-80.1% with accuracy up 0.3-5.0 points. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B overall: DEER 69.2 accuracy at 61.5% tokens vs vanilla 64.2 at 100%. Qwen3-14B overall 83.7 at 57.1% vs vanilla 82.8.
limits: Too-low threshold over-corrects. Llama-3.1-Nemotron-Nano-8B showed weak benefit (appendix). Dynasor-CoT baseline saved only 16% (83.7% tokens).
agent_relevance: Closest existing method to an in-loop 'trial answer then check confidence' stop. Fits S4 test: probe an answer at each reasoning pause.

source: Fu et al. (2025, ICML) Efficiently Scaling LLM Reasoning with Certaindex (Dynasor)
finding: Answer stabilization: intermediate answers stop changing after a point. Certaindex measures this (1 minus normalised entropy of answers across paths; reward-model score for MCTS). High value predicts fewer steps left, so the run can stop early. Built into a serving scheduler.
numbers: Up to 50% compute saved and 3.3x higher throughput with no accuracy drop. Chain-of-thought with reasoning models: token use down 11-29% at the same accuracy; for the top 10% of problems savings of 34% on AIME and 53% on MATH500; top 1% 53% on AIME and 81% on MATH500.
limits: Threshold must be calibrated on a profiling set to avoid hurting accuracy. Authors did not study integration with chunked prefill or disaggregated serving.
agent_relevance: A stop signal that works for chain, vote, and tree search alike. We can read it from our own attempt log.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Use model-internal token confidence to drop weak reasoning traces during generation (stop a trace when its group confidence falls below a threshold set by a warm-up) and to weight votes.
numbers: AIME 2025 with GPT-OSS-120B (no tools): DeepConf@512 99.9% vs 97.0% for majority vote at 512 and 91.8% pass@1; up to 84.7% fewer tokens. At budget 512: DeepConf-low saves 43-84% of tokens, e.g. DeepSeek-8B AIME24 -77.9% tokens +5.8 points; Qwen3-32B AIME24 -66.8% +4.7 points. DeepConf-high saves 16-59% with accuracy about unchanged.
limits: Overconfidence on wrong problems hurts: Qwen3-8B AIME25 -4.4 points; aggressive filtering sometimes hurts GPT-OSS-120B. Needs an offline warm-up and token logprobs.
agent_relevance: Confidence can cut samples but is not safe alone. Matches G4 and G10: a confident model is not a correct one, so keep a code check as the last gate.

source: Liu, Qu, Schneider, Singh, Kumar (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs fail to stop gathering information at the right time, over- or under-shooting. CaRT trains a termination model on counterfactual trajectory pairs (one where stopping is right, one minimally changed where it is not) with a written reason for each.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen3-1.7B. Medical diagnosis dialogue (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as outcome judge, 50 generations per prefix) and DeepScaleR math (2,000 problems). Stop point chosen where success rate rises by 0.5 or more; counterfactual where it drops below 0.3. CaRT beat base and plain SFT on optimal-termination rate and success vs fixed-turn baseline; ablating counterfactuals gave the largest loss. Dermatology out of domain: base and SFT did worse than a fixed-turn rule, CaRT still above it.
limits: Few exact headline numbers in the text read. RL on top of CaRT made conversations longer. Only 3B and 1.7B models, synthetic patient dialogues.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a model cannot judge its own sufficiency without training. Our code-side stop (checks, vote margin) should replace 'do I know enough?' prompts.

source: Russell and Wefald (1991) Principles of Metareasoning / Do the Right Thing; Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis
finding: Rational metareasoning: do a computation only if its expected gain in decision quality exceeds its time cost. Cited by RaM as the root of the value-of-computation reward. Lieder and Griffiths extend it to human strategy choice.
numbers: Not read directly. Only as cited by c10.
limits: Secondary: known only through De Sabbata et al. citation.
agent_relevance: Formal basis for a stop rule: stop when estimated gain from another sample or revision is below its token cost.

source: Li et al. (2024) ESC, control scheme and theory (section 2.3-2.4)
finding: The early stop changes the vote only if the true leader has been outvoted in one window. This chance is small and shrinks fast with window size. Authors derive an expected sample count and a bound on disagreement with full voting, from the first window.
numbers: Window size w0 = 5 recommended for the first calibration window. With w = 8 the chance that the vote differs from full SC is small (bound derived in section 2.3). Table 2 on MATH GPT-4, window 8: cap 16 gives 58.92 accuracy using 13.56 samples; cap 64 gives 60.31 with 42.41 samples.
limits: Assumes samples are independent draws from one answer distribution (violates G4 for correlated errors). Bound is about matching SC, not about being right.
agent_relevance: Stopping preserves the vote but not correctness. If errors are correlated, an early unanimous window can be unanimously wrong.

source: Wang et al. (2025) DSC, ablation and hidden input cost
finding: ASC and ESC cut output samples but can raise input cost, since each new draw re-sends a long few-shot prompt. This can outweigh the savings. DSC pre-allocates sample size per question so most questions get one call.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo input tokens about 846 per question vs output about 164 on GSM8K (cost 0.0004 / 0.0002 USD). GPT-4 prices 0.0254 / 0.0085 USD. Three-step ablation (rank, partition, pre-allocate) each lowers cost.
limits: Input cost matters mostly with long few-shot prompts and cached prompts change this.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold prompts are long. Count total tokens including prompt, or use prompt caching, before claiming savings.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Overthinking paper, efficiency metrics and diversity result
finding: Two metrics: outcome efficiency (share of tokens used up to the first correct answer) and process efficiency (share of later solutions that add a distinct approach). Later rounds are mostly repeats.
numbers: Over 92% of cases correct in first round. Easiest set ASDiv first solution about 287 tokens. o1-like models make 2-4 rounds in 76-80% of cases (QwQ) and 59-63% (R1).
limits: Definition of a 'distinct' solution is judged by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Gives measurable quantities for G7: tokens spent after the first passing check are waste on easy items.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Section 7: pretraining versus test-time trade
finding: Where the base model already has some success, test-time compute can replace a bigger model. Where it has almost none, extra thinking does little.
numbers: FLOPs-matched against a 14x larger model; test-time compute better on easy and intermediate bins and at low inference load; pretraining better on the hardest bin or high load.
quote: on problems where a smaller base model attains somewhat non-trivial success rates
limits: Compute estimates from one model family; relies on PRM verifier for search.
agent_relevance: Directly supports the G12 foothold rule: do not pour samples into a problem class with near-zero success.

source: Kim et al. (2026) ReASC, two-stage analysis (Stage 1 acceptance, Table 2-3)
finding: A single-sample confidence check accepts a share of items at high accuracy. Larger models accept more. Items passed on must still go to the vote.
numbers: GSM8K offline acceptance ratio 48.98% (Llama-3.2-3B, accuracy of accepted 91.33), 51.18% (Gemma-3-4B, 97.78), 59.59% (Qwen-2.5-7B, 97.58), 60.58% (Gemma-3-27B, 98.62). MATH500 offline acceptance 7.2% for Llama-3.2-3B (accepted accuracy 86.11), 34.0% Gemma-3-4B (96.47). Target accuracy 0.9.
limits: Calibration uses held-out data (128 items). Online variant accepts fewer on GSM8K (28 to 41%).
agent_relevance: A one-sample gate (S0/S3) is worth keeping for easy classes; for hard ones it accepts little and adds only a small cost.

source: Yang et al. (2025) DEER, ablation on trigger and threshold
finding: Trigger can be a keyword ('Wait') or an entropy spike. Threshold matters: too low cuts reasoning short, too high saves little. A single value of 0.95 worked across 10 datasets.
numbers: Qwen3-14B overall accuracy 83.7 at 57.1% of tokens (DEER) vs 82.8 at 100% (vanilla); thinking-off baseline NoThinking 66.9 at 34.1%; Chain of Draft 68.9 at 51.4%. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B on GPQA-D: DEER 31.3 at 53.4% tokens vs vanilla 23.7.
limits: Threshold sensitivity shown on MATH-500 only; some models (Nemotron-Nano) gave little gain.
agent_relevance: Prefer probing mid-run to hard caps: NoThinking loses 15 to 17 points overall, DEER loses none.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Certaindex, correlation test and thresholding
finding: Higher certaindex predicts fewer remaining steps to the final answer, tested on Llama and QwQ with GSM8K and across CoT, self-consistency, MCTS and REBASE. A threshold at a chosen reasoning step halts any query above it.
numbers: Self-consistency, MCTS and REBASE reasoning programs saved tokens at the same accuracy (figures of 7B/14B/32B models; exact values not recorded). Policy threshold is set by profiling so accuracy on calibration data is not hurt.
limits: Profiling needs a labelled calibration set per task.
agent_relevance: A calibrated agreement threshold per problem class is cheap to keep in our class lookup (S0).

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency; Wei et al. (2022) CoT, as cited by Adaptive-Consistency and ESC
finding: Fixed-budget voting: sample 40 chains and take the majority. Accuracy rises quickly then plateaus. All the stopping papers measure themselves against this.
numbers: Not opened. Used as baseline sample size 40 in c01 and c04.
limits: Baseline only.
agent_relevance: Fixed 40 is the cost ceiling to beat.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: stop rules compared (c01, c04, c06, c07)
finding: Savings on GSM8K versus full self-consistency by method: ASC about 60%, ESC about 60%, ReASC about 70%, DSC about 56-65% (different models and baselines). All keep accuracy within about one point. Savings shrink on hard sets (GPQA, MATH500).
limits: Comparison across different papers; baselines and prompts differ. Only the ReASC numbers are one controlled table.
agent_relevance: Plan for 55 to 70% fewer samples on easy math, 15 to 35% on hard ones.

source: Fu et al. (2025) DeepConf, ablation on warm-up size and online/offline mode
finding: Online mode stops traces mid-generation using a threshold from warm-up traces (percentile of lowest group confidence). Warm-up size changes savings. Also an early-stop on vote agreement was tested.
numbers: Warm-up sizes 8, 16, 32 compared at budget 512 (Table 4). Largest cost reduction 43-84% fewer tokens than majority at B=512. Exceptions: Qwen3-8B/AIME25 -4.4 points, small drops under 1 point on GPT-OSS BRUMO and HMMT.
limits: Needs a full-length warm-up first; saves less on easy sets where all traces are confident.
agent_relevance: A warm-up of a few full attempts, then cheaper attempts, fits our S3 generate step.
